passage_text: Researchers investigated how different visual cues affect reaction times in a simple choice task. A total of 120 undergraduate participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: Control (no cue), Condition A (a red cue), Condition B (a blue cue), and Condition C (a green cue). Each participant completed 50 trials, and the mean reaction time (RT) and standard deviation (SD) were recorded. The Control group had a mean RT of 650 ms (SD = 45 ms), Condition A had 630 ms (SD = 50 ms), Condition B had 615 ms (SD = 48 ms), and Condition C had 640 ms (SD = 47 ms). The researchers hypothesized that color cues would reduce reaction times compared to the Control. The data were analyzed using a one‑way ANOVA, followed by post‑hoc Tukey tests to identify significant pairwise differences. The results indicated that Condition B produced the fastest responses, significantly faster than Control, while Condition A did not differ significantly from Control. The authors concluded that blue visual cues may facilitate faster perceptual processing in this task.
stem: Which condition had the lowest mean reaction time according to the study?
explanation: The table shows Condition B with a mean RT of 615 ms, the lowest among all conditions.
trap: Some may confuse the SD values with mean values or overlook the fact that the lowest mean is 615 ms.

stem: Which experimental design best supports the conclusion that blue cues reduce reaction time?

options.A: A within‑subject crossover design where each participant experiences all four conditions.
options.B: A between‑subject randomized controlled design with equal group sizes.
options.C: A correlational design measuring natural variations in color preference.
options.D: An observational design where participants choose their preferred cue color.

explanation: A randomized controlled between‑subject design controls for individual differences and allows causal inference about the effect of cue color.
trap: The trap is to think that a within‑subject design is always superior; however, it can introduce carry‑over effects in reaction‑time tasks.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: Condition B had the lowest mean reaction time (615 ms).
options.B: Condition A did not differ significantly from Control.
options.C: Blue cues speed up reaction times in all people and in all kinds of tasks.
options.D: Standard deviations were similar across conditions (45 to 50 ms).

explanation: Correct: C) The study tested undergraduates on one simple choice task, so it cannot show an effect in all people and all tasks. Why the others are wrong: A) 615 ms is the lowest mean in the table. B) The passage states Condition A did not differ significantly from Control. D) The SDs range from 45 to 50 ms.
trap: Generalizing a significant effect in undergraduates on one simple task to all people and all tasks.

stem: By what percent was the mean reaction time in Condition B lower than in the Control group?
explanation: Correct: A) (650 - 615)/650 x 100 = 5.4%. Why the others are wrong: B) 5.7% divides the 35 ms difference by the Condition B mean (615) instead of the Control mean. C) 3.1% is the Condition A difference (20 ms) over the Control mean. D) 35 is the difference in milliseconds, not a percent.
trap: Dividing the 35 ms difference by the Condition B mean (35/615 = 5.7%) instead of the Control baseline, or reporting 35 ms as a percent.
